To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the adrenal gland responds normally to ACTH stimulation in PTSD patients.
the adrenocortico-steroid response to ACTH is normal in PTSD and that the adrenal androgen response is not abnormal.
PTSD patients show normal adrenocortial responsiveness to low dose ACTH and that the adrenal androgen DHEA is not increased in PTSD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the hypothalomo-pituitary-adrenocortical axis in posttraumatic stress disorders (PTSD).
the study of the hypothalmo–pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis in patients with posttraumatic stress disorders (PTSD).
the neurobiology of posttraumatic psychopathology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the HPA axis in PTSD is not abnormal, but that the disorder can be associated with a variety of HPA axis abnormalities, depending on the type of trauma, the type of stress response, and the genetic susceptibility of the individual.
the HPA axis in PTSD is not abnormal, but rather, is normal, and that the HPA dysfunction that is reported is secondary to the PTSD.
PTSD is not associated with a specific defect in the regulation of cortisol secretion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adrenal cortex is not abnormal in PTSD.
there is no evidence for PTSD-specific alterations in adrenocortisol responsiveness to physiological doses of ACTHA.
the HPA axis in PTSD is not abnormal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HPA axis is not a biomarker for PTSD.
the adrenal cortex in PTSD patients has the same sensitivity to physiological doses of ACTHT as in control subjects.
there is no single abnormality in the regulation of the HPA axis in PTSD.
